In twenty nineteen, one office company was worth forty-seven billion dollars. It didn't invent anything. It rented offices. This is how WeWork rose, and fell. In twenty ten, Adam Neumann and Miguel McKelvey opened their first shared office in New York. The idea was simple: take a long lease on a building, fill it with glass walls, beer on tap and free coffee, then rent the desks out, month by month. Adam didn't sell desks. He sold a dream. WeWork was a community, he said, that would elevate the world's consciousness. Investors loved it. Then SoftBank's boss, Masayoshi Son, put in billions of dollars. WeWork spread to hundreds of buildings in dozens of countries, and by early twenty nineteen, it was valued at forty-seven billion. There was just one problem. It was losing money. A lot of money.
